chapter.title: Values Across the Bridge
chapter.para: Objects cross the bridge by reference: a Python list used from Rexx is the list itself, never a copy. Only strings and numbers are converted, because each language has its own. This chapter is the one rule worth learning before anything else.

section.title: What Crosses as a String, What Stays an Object
section.para: You want to know what you get back from Python, and what Python gets from you.

How it works. Coming back from Python, str, int and float are Rexx strings, a bool is .LogicalWrapper~true or .LogicalWrapper~false, which Rexx takes as 1 and 0, and None is .nil. Everything else, a dict here, stays in Python and comes to Rexx as a PyObject, a reference to it: its Rexx class is PyObject, and its Python type is dict.

Going to Python, a Rexx string that is a number goes as a number: 42 as an int, 3.5 as a float. Anything else goes as a str, and so does a number written in a way Python would not write it: "007" stays text. This is the number rule, and it is needed because Python, unlike Rexx, never turns text into a number by itself: math~sqrt("2") would fail in Python.
.py~str(42) makes a Python str and keeps it as a PyObject, so that Python's string methods, such as zfill, can be used on it.

section.title: Text that Looks Like a Number
section.para: You want to pass "2026" as text, a file name, and not as a number.

How it works. By the number rule, 2026 goes as an int, which join refuses. There are two ways out. For one value, .py~str(2026) makes it a str. For a module that works mostly with such text, .py~import("posixpath", "string") sends every Rexx string as a str in every call through the module and through what it returns. Positions and keys in o[k] keep the number rule, so parts[0] is still the first item.
The sample uses posixpath, the Unix flavour of os.path, so that it prints the same on Windows.
See also Reference, Modules that Want Strings.

section.title: Choosing the Python Type
section.para: You want a float, bytes, a fraction or a decimal, not what the number rule picks.

How it works. py.box(type, value), with BSF4ooRexx's argument order (also .py~box(type, value)), makes a Python object of that type from the value's text, and keeps it as a PyObject, so that passing it on keeps its type. The types are str, int, float, bool, bytes, complex, decimal, fraction, or a Python class. Python's operators work on the results, so two fractions add up as fractions, and two decimals as decimals, without float's rounding.
